# Choosing Between Methods {#comparison}

::: {.callout-note}
## Section Overview

**What you will learn:** A comprehensive decision guide for choosing between hierarchical clustering, k-means, and CA based on your data type and research question; a full comparison table; and a recommended step-by-step analytical workflow
:::

## Decision Guide {-}

```{r comp_table, echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
data.frame(
  Dimension = c(
    "Input data type", "Requires specifying k?",
    "Output", "Visualisation options",
    "Handles mixed data types?", "Scalability (N objects)",
    "Bootstrap validation?", "Detects non-spherical clusters?",
    "Provides significance test?", "Shows direction of association?",
    "Best linguistic use case"
  ),
  `Hierarchical\n(hclust)` = c(
    "Numeric, binary, mixed (Gower)", "No — decided post-hoc",
    "Dendrogram + membership",
    "Dendrogram, heat map, ape phylo, fviz_dend",
    "Yes (with Gower distance)", "Moderate (< ~1,000)",
    "Yes (pvclust)", "Yes (single linkage)",
    "No", "No (use mean diff plots)",
    "Dialect/language typology; EME register; exploratory analysis"
  ),
  `k-Means\n(kmeans)` = c(
    "Continuous numeric only", "Yes — before fitting",
    "Flat partition + centroids",
    "fviz_cluster, silhouette plot",
    "No", "High (millions)",
    "No (use bootstrap externally)", "No — spherical only",
    "No", "No (use centroid plots)",
    "Large-scale text clustering; speaker segmentation; confirmation of HCA"
  ),
  `Correspondence\nAnalysis (CA)` = c(
    "Contingency table (counts)", "Not applicable",
    "Row + column coordinates",
    "Biplot, scree plot, contribution plots",
    "No", "Moderate",
    "No", "Not applicable",
    "Yes (chi-squared)", "Yes — in biplot",
    "Amplifier/collocation patterns; L2 error profiles; register × feature associations"
  ),
  check.names = FALSE
) |>
  flextable() |>
  flextable::set_table_properties(width = 1, layout = "autofit") |>
  flextable::theme_zebra() |>
  flextable::fontsize(size = 9) |>
  flextable::bold(part = "header") |>
  flextable::set_caption("Full comparison: hierarchical clustering vs. k-Means vs. CA")
```

## Recommended Analytical Workflow {-}

**Step 1 — Assess clusterability (Hopkins statistic)**
Before any clustering, confirm the data contains genuine structure. If Hopkins ≈ 0.5, the data is too random for meaningful clustering.

**Step 2 — Choose the distance measure**
Match the measure to your data type: Euclidean/Manhattan for scaled numeric; binary (Jaccard) for presence/absence; Gower for mixed types.

**Step 3 — Hierarchical clustering (exploratory)**
Fit with `ward.D2` linkage. Compare linkage methods with cophenetic correlation. Choose k using silhouette + elbow + gap statistic. Validate with `pvclust` (nboot = 1000). Visualise with dendrogram and heat map.

**Step 4 — k-Means (confirmation / large N)**
Fit with `nstart = 25`. Compare to hierarchical solution. Flag borderline objects where the two methods disagree.

**Step 5 — Identify distinctive features**
Compute mean feature differences per cluster, visualise as barplot. For nominal data, run Fisher's exact tests. Report which features most strongly define each cluster.

**Step 6 — Correspondence analysis (if you have a contingency table)**
Run chi-squared first. Interpret eigenvalues and scree plot. Produce biplot with row/column contributions. Interpret each dimension as an association gradient.

```{r comp_q8, echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, results='asis'}
check_question(
  "A researcher has a corpus of 500,000 words tagged for 8 amplifiers and wants to see how 40 adjectives differ in their amplifier preferences. She also has a separate dataset of 30 dialect varieties described by 15 continuous phonological features. Which methods should she use for each dataset?",
  options = c(
    "CA for both datasets — it handles all contingency and continuous data",
    "Hierarchical clustering for both — it is always the safest choice",
    "For the amplifier/adjective data: CA on the contingency table (it is specifically designed for categorical co-occurrence counts and produces a biplot showing both amplifiers and adjectives). For the dialect data: hierarchical clustering (with scaled Euclidean distance and ward.D2 linkage) followed optionally by k-means for confirmation — suitable for continuous numeric data with moderate N.",
    "k-Means for the amplifier data (large dataset) and CA for the dialect data"
  ),
  answer = "For the amplifier/adjective data: CA on the contingency table (it is specifically designed for categorical co-occurrence counts and produces a biplot showing both amplifiers and adjectives). For the dialect data: hierarchical clustering (with scaled Euclidean distance and ward.D2 linkage) followed optionally by k-means for confirmation — suitable for continuous numeric data with moderate N.",
  type   = "radio",
  right  = "Correct! The key is matching the method to the data type and research question. The amplifier/adjective cross-tabulation is a contingency table of co-occurrence counts — exactly the input CA is designed for. CA will show amplifiers and adjectives simultaneously in one biplot, revealing which amplifiers are preferred with which adjectives. The dialect dataset is continuous numeric data (phonological features) — hierarchical clustering with Euclidean distance is appropriate. k-Means can then confirm the hierarchical solution.",
  wrong  = "Not quite. The choice of method should be driven by the data type. The amplifier/adjective data is a contingency table — CA is the appropriate method. The dialect data is continuous numeric — hierarchical clustering (and optionally k-means) is appropriate. CA requires a contingency table; cluster methods require a distance matrix from numeric, binary, or mixed data."
)
```

```{r citation-bibtex, echo=FALSE, results='asis'}
key <- paste0(
  tolower(gsub(" ", "", gsub(",.*", "", params$author))),
  params$year,
  tolower(gsub("[^a-zA-Z]", "", strsplit(params$title, " ")[[1]][1]))
)

cat("@manual{", key, ",\n",           sep = "")
